    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):
            metrics['input_range_ok'] = bool(
                mean_input_range_error <= STATLIMITS['input_range_error'])
    
        # match outputs based on range, fraction, and semantic similarity of names
        output_matches, output_match_costs = match_outputs(
            submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
        )
        metrics['output_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in output_matches
        ]
    
        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))
        metrics['output_match_mean_cost'] = mean_output_match_cost
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']
        ref_output_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_output_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])
    
        for field in fields_check:

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None

                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],

        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)

            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])

        }

        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be

        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy

        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None

            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a

                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:

                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio

            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}

            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.

                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy

            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return

        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.

        # not before the metric has been recorded.

            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.

            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).

                    continue

            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio

A decision that differs from the expert's is acceptable if it is equally well justified; decisions that are poorly justified will be flagged as concerning or incorrect.\n\n## Reference Information\n\n- Reference **papers**:\n  - The whitepaper about the dataset, \"Allen Brain Observatory: Visual Behavior 2P Technical Whitepaper\", is in the file `/app/whitepaper.pdf`.\n  - A paper using this dataset, \"Behavioral strategy shapes activation of the Vip-Sst disinhibitory circuit in visual cortex\", is in the file `/app/paper.pdf`.\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n- **Code**:\n  - The Allen data **SDK** is in the directory `/app/code`.\n  - Tutorials about using the data are in the directory `/app/tutorials`.\n- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `/app/data`.\n\n## Decoder Task\n\n- Collect and convert data under the \"Visual Behavior\" task.\n- Temporally align based on ophys timestamp.\n- Segment each recording session into individual trials based on how they are defined in the experiment. Include both the \"Go\" and \"Catch\" trials, but exclude the \"Aborted\" and \"Auto-rewarded\" trials.\n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n\nNo inputs for this task.\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n\n- Image identity (of the image presented during the non-grey screen), categorical variable. Time-varying.\n- Image change, binary variable. Have value of 1 right after a change in image identity, otherwise 0. Time-varying.\n- Running speed, discretized into five equal percentile bins. Time-varying.\n- Pupil diameter, discretized into five equal percentile bins.  Time-varying.\n- Trial outcome. Static per-trial.\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. During testing, a reference copy of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. The full trial window (`start_time` to `stop_time`) is used rather than a fixed window around `change_time`, so that the trial includes both pre-change stimulus flashes and the post-change response window. This enables time-varying output variables (image identity changes mid-trial). Since the trial window now spans both pre- and post-change periods, image identity varies within a trial. Before `change_time`, the initial image is on screen; after, the change image is displayed. A global mapping ensures consistent integer codes across sessions. Sorting the image names makes the mapping deterministic. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Image change* derived from?\n\ni. Image change is a binary time-varying variable derived from `change_time` and the `go` column in the trials table. For catch trials (sham change), `image_change` is 0 throughout.\n\nii.\n```python\nimage_change = np.zeros(n_frames, dtype=np.int8)\nif row['go']:\n    change_end_idx = np.searchsorted(ophys_ts[idx], row['change_time'] + 0.75)\n    image_change[change_idx:change_end_idx] = 1\n```\n\niii. The 750ms window corresponds to one stimulus flash (250ms) plus the following grey inter-stimulus interval (500ms). This marks only the transient change event rather than the entire post-change period. Catch trials are excluded because no actual image change occurs — the `go` column distinguishes real changes from sham changes.\n\n## 4-b. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. Yes — the native ophys sampling is rebinned to a uniform **100 ms** bin (`metadata['time_bin_size'] = 100.0`), giving 72 bins per trial for all 51,992 trials. This is a ~3× downsampling for the single-plane experiments (30.95 Hz) and a ~1.07× rebin for the multiscope plane-files (10.7 Hz); the uniform grid is what makes those two populations dimensionally compatible. Rebinning is by mean over the frames falling in each bin.\n\nii.\n```python\nDT=0.100\nNB=int(round((OFF1-OFF0)/DT))\n...\n            bi=np.floor((tt-edges[0])/DT).astype(int)\n            for k in range(NB):\n                z=slab[bi==k]\n                if len(z): mat[:,k]=z.mean(axis=0)\n...\n          'metadata':{...,'time_bin_size':DT*1000,...}\n```\n\niii. \"Native-frame data would create a very large pickle; 100 ms bins preserve calcium-event and behavior dynamics while making the complete dataset tractable\" and \"To keep the complete active-task dataset tractable while respecting temporal alignment, 100 ms bins are appropriate for the relatively slow calcium-event signal.\" (The resulting pickle is still 2.3 GB.)\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Image identity* derived from?\n\ni. Class 0 is an explicit \"gray\" (inter-flash blank) category, giving 17 categories.\n\nii.\n```python\n    image_values=['gray']+[f'{s}_image_{i}' for s in ('A','B') for i in range(8)]\n...\n        setoff=1 if 'images_A' in stype else 9\n...\n        preskeys=list(h['stimulus/presentation'].keys())\n        pg=h['stimulus/presentation/'+preskeys[0]]\n        stim_t=np.asarray(pg['timestamps'],dtype=float); stim_i=np.asarray(pg['data'])\n```\n\niii. \"Image identity will include gray plus all natural images\"; code comment: \"Global categorical image names are index-defined separately for familiar and novel sets, hence prefix by set A/B. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Image identity*?\n\ni. For each 100 ms bin center, the most recent flash onset is found; the bin is labelled with that flash's image (offset by the set code) only if the center falls within 250 ms of the onset — otherwise it is labelled gray (0). Indices ≥ 8 (the \"omitted\" code) are also forced to gray; in these files the presentation TimeSeries already excludes omitted flashes (4610 entries vs 4806 table rows), so omissions fall out as gray automatically because the gap to the previous onset is 1.5 s. The result is a 17-class time series in which each 750 ms flash cycle appears as 2–3 image bins followed by 5 gray bins (≈68% of all bins are gray).\n\nii.\n```python\n            # Screen is gray except during [onset,onset+.25). Derived from the whitepaper's stimulus structure (250 ms image, 500 ms gray, 750 ms cycle): \"derive image timing from stimulus presentation TimeSeries\" and \"Image identity will include gray plus all natural images\".\n\n## 3-c. A single bin is set to 1 — the bin whose center is closest to `change_time` — and all other 71 bins are 0. Bin 29 spans `[change_time − 0.1 s, change_time)`, i.e. the pulse lands in the bin immediately **before** the change, one bin earlier than the image-identity switch at bin 30 (the tie between bins 29 and 30, both 50 ms from the change, is broken toward the earlier one by `argmin`).\n\nii.\n```python\n            ch=np.zeros(NB,dtype=np.int16); ch[np.argmin(abs(centers-change[j]))]=1\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Running speed*?\n\ni. Non-finite samples are masked out, then the speed is **linearly interpolated onto the 100 ms bin centers** of each trial (`np.interp`, which clamps rather than extrapolates outside the recorded span). No smoothing, rectification or absolute value; negative speeds are retained and simply fall into the lowest quintile. The interpolated value is then quintile-binned (see 5-c).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef interp_clean(t,x,q):\n    t=np.asarray(t); x=np.asarray(x,dtype=float)\n    good=np.isfinite(t)&np.isfinite(x)\n    if good.sum()<2: return np.zeros(len(q),dtype=np.float32)\n    return np.interp(q,t[good],x[good]).astype(np.float32)\n...\n            run=interp_clean(rt,rv,centers)\n```\n\niii. \"Running and pupil diameter will be interpolated and session-wide percentile-binned\"; the running encoder samples at ~60 Hz, far faster than the 10 Hz bin grid, so interpolation at bin centers is a faithful resampling.\n\n## 5-c. How is `output` *Running speed* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Into five quintile bins, with the quintile edges (20/40/60/80th percentiles) computed **per session from the entire session's running trace** (not from the trial-restricted values, and not pooled across sessions), then applied with `np.digitize`. Realized global distribution is 0.197 / 0.207 / 0.207 / 0.204 / 0.185 — close to but not exactly 20% each, because edges are derived from whole-session data and applied only to the trial windows.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef quintile_reference(x):\n    x=np.asarray(x,dtype=float); x=x[np.isfinite(x)]\n    if len(x)==0: return np.array([-np.inf]*4)\n    return np.quantile(x,[.2,.4,.6,.8])\n...\n        rq=quintile_reference(rv)\n...\n            runbin=np.digitize(run,rq).astype(np.int16)\n```\n```python\n          'metadata':{...,'behavior_binning':'within-session quintiles; pupil diameter is tracked pupil width',...}\n```\n\niii. \"quintile-bin continuous behavior per session\"; documented in metadata as \"within-session quintiles\". Per-session edges normalize away between-session/between-animal differences in locomotion level so that each session contributes balanced classes.\n\n## 5-d. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Handled: (a) NaN/inf samples in running speed and pupil width are masked out before interpolation, which also removes blink frames; (b) trials with NaN `change_time` are dropped; (c) sessions with <2 valid trials are not emitted; (d) a missing `EyeTracking` group is tolerated (no crash); (e) the brain-region lookup falls back to the string `'visual cortex'` if no imaging-plane `location` attribute is found; (f) `stim_i` values ≥8 (omitted flashes) are forced to gray, and bins before the first flash are gray. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. (1) The `for k in range(NB)` bin loop, which builds a boolean mask over the slab 72 times per trial; it could be replaced by a single `np.add.reduceat` / `np.bincount`-weighted reduction over the frame-to-bin index, or by `(counts, sums) = np.bincount(bi, ...)`. (2) The outer `for j in keep` trial loop: `edges`/`centers` for all trials could be computed as one (n_trials, 73) array, and `interp_clean`, `np.digitize`, the stimulus `searchsorted`, and the change-flag assignment could all be done once per session on flattened center arrays instead of per trial. (3) `np.argmin(abs(centers-change[j]))` recomputes a constant (always 29) 51,992 times. (4) The `subjects` set comprehension re-opens every file instead of reusing the metadata already read in the filter pass.\n\nii.\n```python\n            mat=np.zeros((ncell,NB),dtype=np.float32)\n            bi=np.floor((tt-edges[0])/DT).astype(int)\n            for k in range(NB):\n                z=slab[bi==k]\n                if len(z): mat[:,k]=z.mean(axis=0)\n```\n```python\n        for j in keep:\n            edges=change[j]+OFF0+np.arange(NB+1)*DT\n            centers=(edges[:-1]+edges[1:])/2\n```\n\niii. No justification is given; the AI never profiled the inner loop and its efficiency reasoning stopped at avoiding the SDK's eager loading.\n\n## 9-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. (1) Every NWB is opened and its scalar metadata decoded up to three times (session-type filter, subject-id comprehension, main loop) — and the comprehension's file handles are never closed. (2) `np.arange(NB+1)*DT` and the bin-center arithmetic are rebuilt for each of the 51,992 trials although only the offset changes. (3) `np.argmin(abs(centers-change[j]))` recomputes the same constant index every trial. (4) For multiscope sessions, the *same* behavioral and stimulus processing (trial table, running interpolation, pupil interpolation, quintile edges, image identity, outcomes) is redone independently for each of the 3–7 plane files of the same physical session, and the identical resulting label matrices are stored 3–7 times in the output. (5) `np.clip(pos,0,len(stim_t)-1)` and the `stim_i[pp]<8` test are evaluated per trial though the presentation arrays are session-constant.\n\nii.\n```python\n    subjects=sorted({text(h5py.File(f,'r')['general/subject/subject_id']) for f in files})\n```\n```python\n            edges=change[j]+OFF0+np.arange(NB+1)*DT\n            ...\n            ch=np.zeros(NB,dtype=np.int16); ch[np.argmin(abs(centers-change[j]))]=1\n```\n\niii. Not discussed in the trajectory; the duplicated multiscope work is a direct consequence of the \"each NWB is a session\" decision (1-c), which the AI reaffirmed after noticing the \"identical trial counts\".\n\n## 9-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\ni. (1) An empty `(0, 72)` float32 array is allocated and stored for every one of the 51,992 trials as the decoder input, although the task has no inputs. (2) The static trial outcome is materialized as 72 identical values per trial. (3) The `stim_i[pp]<8` guard is dead code — the presentation TimeSeries in these files only contains indices 0–7 (omitted flashes are absent from it). (4) The full pupil stream is read, interpolated and quintiled for the three sessions where the result is a constant, meaningless label. (5) `image_values` always carries all 17 A+B labels even though a given session can only produce 9 of them. Auto-rewarded trials were excluded because the free reward biases the behavioral response. Requiring a valid `change_time` ensures there is a well-defined change point within the trial. Image name is a time-varying variable derived from both `initial_image_name` and `change_image_name` columns in the trials table, combined with `change_time` to determine when the image switches.\n\nii.\n```python\nchange_idx = np.searchsorted(ophys_ts[idx], row['change_time'])\nimage_names = np.empty(n_frames, dtype=object)\nimage_names[:change_idx] = row['initial_image_name']\nimage_names[change_idx:] = row['change_image_name']\n```\n\niii. This marks only the transient change event rather than the entire post-change period. Catch trials are excluded because no actual image change occurs — the `go` column distinguishes real changes from sham changes.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Trial outcome*?\n\ni. Trial outcomes are mapped to integer codes (0–3) via a fixed mapping. The integer code is constant across all time bins within a trial.\n\nii.\n```python\noutcome_to_code = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(TRIAL_OUTCOMES)}\n...\noutcome_code = outcome_to_code.get(t['trial_outcome'], -1)\noutcome_row = np.full(n_frames, outcome_code, dtype=np.int8)\n```\n\niii. The mapping order matches `TRIAL_OUTCOMES = ['hit', 'miss', 'false_alarm', 'correct_reject']`. The mapping is stored in `metadata['outcome_to_code']` for recovery.\n\n## 8. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several cases are handled:\n- **Failed sessions**: If `extract_session_data` or `segment_trials` throws an exception, the session is skipped with a warning.\n- **Truncated trials**: If `stop_time` extends past the recording, the trial is clipped to the end. Trials with no frames (`end_idx <= start_idx`) are skipped.\n- **Missing behavioral data**: NaN values from interpolation (running speed or pupil diameter outside the recorded range) are mapped to bin 0 during discretization.\n- **Few trials**: Sessions with fewer than 2 valid trials are excluded.\n\nii.\n```python\ntry:\n    session_data = extract_session_data(bc, sess_exps)\n    trials = segment_trials(session_data)\nexcept Exception as e:\n    print(f'FAILED: {e}')\n    continue\n...\nif end_idx > T:\n    end_idx = T\nif end_idx <= start_idx:\n    continue\n...\nout[np.isnan(values)] = 0\n...\nif len(trials) < 2:\n    continue\n```\n\niii. The try/except ensures a single bad session doesn't crash the entire pipeline. NaN-to-0 mapping is a conservative default that avoids propagating missing data into the discretized output.\n\n## 9-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. The most time-consuming step is loading each experiment via `bc.get_behavior_ophys_experiment()`, which downloads/reads large neural and behavioral data arrays from the S3 cache. This is I/O bound.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. Each experiment contains full-session dF/F traces for all neurons, plus running speed, eye tracking, and trials data. The SDK caches files locally after first download, but reading them is still the bottleneck.\n\n## 9-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. The per-trial loop in `segment_trials` iterates over each valid trial sequentially. The `np.searchsorted` and array slicing could theoretically be vectorized across all trials, but the loop is not a bottleneck compared to data loading.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The per-trial loop is simple and readable. Data loading dominates runtime, so vectorizing the trial loop would yield negligible speedup.\n\n## 9-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\nNo processing is repeated. Each session is loaded once in Pass 1, and the extracted trial data is reused for discretization (bin edge computation) and final assembly without reloading.\n\n## 9-d. Only small metadata (`ophys_ts`, `plane_labels`) is retained for later use. The trial-level slices (already copied during `segment_trials`) are the only data kept.\n\nii.\n```python\nsession_meta = {\n    'ophys_ts': session_data['ophys_ts'],\n    'plane_labels': session_data['plane_labels'],\n}\ndel session_data\nsession_results.append((mouse_id, session_meta, trials))\n```\n\niii.
